stage1_rawInput.title: Ma che dici?

items.it: Aspetta un momentino, me lo devi spiegare perché io non ho capito proprio niente.
items.en: Wait a moment, you have to explain it to me because I really didn't understand anything at all.
But how do you do it? / But how is it done?

items.it: Perché gli italiani parlano con le mani?
items.en: Why do Italians talk with their hands?

items.it: Parlare con le mani è bello, è divertentissimo.
items.en: Talking with your hands is beautiful, it's really fun.
But what are you saying? / What do you mean?

items.it: Mamma mia, non ci posso credere!
items.en: Oh my goodness, I can't believe it!

anchors: Dropped subjects: Italian often omits subject pronouns (like 'I', 'you') when the verb conjugation makes it clear who is performing the action. E.g., 'Aspetta' (you wait), 'non ho capito' (I didn't understand), 'che dici' (you say), 'non ci posso credere' (I can't believe).

Pre-verb pronouns: 'me lo devi spiegare' literally means 'to me it you must explain'. Pronouns like 'me' (to me) and 'lo' (it) often come before the conjugated verb, especially with modal verbs like 'dovere' (to have to) + infinitive.

Double negation: 'non ho capito proprio niente' uses 'non' before the verb and 'niente' (nothing) after to emphasize 'not anything at all' or 'nothing at all'. 'Proprio' further strengthens the emphasis ('really nothing').
Impersonal 'si': 'Ma come si fa?' means 'But how does one do it?' or 'How is it done?'. The 'si' makes the action general or passive, similar to 'one' or 'it is'.
Infinitive as subject: 'Parlare con le mani è bello' uses the infinitive 'parlare' (to talk/talking) as the subject of the sentence, which is common in Italian.
Superlative suffix '-issimo': 'divertentissimo' means 'very fun' or 'extremely fun'. The suffix '-issimo' (or '-issima', '-issimi', '-issime') is used to form the absolute superlative.

Idiomatic expressions: 'Ma che dici?' is a very common way to say 'What are you saying?' or 'What do you mean?' (often implying disbelief or disagreement). 'Mamma mia!' is an exclamation similar to 'Oh my goodness!' or 'Wow!'.
Pronoun 'ci': 'non ci posso credere' uses 'ci' which often means 'to it/them' or 'there'. Here, it refers to the situation or statement, so it's 'I can't believe it'.

step0_umbrella.frame: Asking 'What do you say/mean?' and expressing disbelief

step5_writeOutput.prompt: Imagine you are the woman. Write two sentences expressing your confusion and disbelief about talking with hands, using phrases from the transcript.

aliveQA.question: Hai mai visto qualcuno parlare con le mani in modo molto espressivo? Cosa hai pensato?

gentleFeedback.thoughtSlice: The learner might struggle with the natural flow and idiomatic expressions, especially 'Ma che dici?' and the double negation. They might also confuse the different uses of 'si'.
gentleFeedback.modelAnswer: Benissimo! You've picked up on the key expressions of confusion and disbelief. When we say 'Ma che dici?', we're often expressing surprise or disagreement, much like 'What are you talking about?' or 'You're kidding!'. And 'non ci posso credere' is perfect for that strong disbelief. Remember how 'ci' adds that little 'to it' to 'believe' in Italian – 'credere a qualcosa' (to believe in something), so 'non ci posso credere' (I can't believe in it).
